'''Herbs, Gems and Gods: How They Go Together''' is the text behind the herbal card set: what each plant does, the compounds and enzymes behind it, how strong the evidence is, the dose, and what it interacts with; then the gemstones and planetary gods that old healers used as the memory system around the plants. Evidence is kept in three honest grades: '''established''', '''traditional with some evidence''', and '''traditional only'''. Gem and planet correspondences are tradition, not medicine.

== Herbs ==
=== Ginger (''Zingiber officinale'') ===
* '''Traditions:''' folk-European, TCM, Ayurveda, Unani
* '''Used for:''' nausea (pregnancy, motion, post-operative, chemotherapy adjunct); dyspepsia; menstrual pain; osteoarthritis pain (modest)
* '''Compounds:''' 6-gingerol, 6-shogaol (forms on drying/heating), zingerone, zingiberene
* '''Mechanism:''' Gingerols and shogaols inhibit COX-2 and 5-LOX (dual eicosanoid suppression) and antagonise gut 5-HT3 receptors, which is the main proposed anti-nausea route; fresh rhizome also carries zingibain, a cysteine protease (bromelain-like meat tenderiser), though it is not the active anti-emetic principle.
* '''Evidence:''' established. Reasonable trial support for pregnancy nausea (included in the Cochrane review of NVP interventions, with low-certainty but consistent benefit) and an EMA well-established/traditional monograph for motion sickness; evidence for arthritis pain is weaker.<ref>[https://www.nccih.nih.gov/health/ginger NCCIH: Ginger]</ref><ref>[https://www.ema.europa.eu/en/medicines/herbal/zingiberis-rhizoma EMA HMPC: Zingiberis rhizoma]</ref><ref>[https://www.cochrane.org/evidence/CD007575 Cochrane: Interventions for nausea and vomiting in early pregnancy (CD007575)]</ref><ref>[https://www.gutenberg.org/ebooks/49513 Nicholas Culpeper, The Complete Herbal (Project Gutenberg eBook #49513)]</ref>
* '''Dose:''' Nausea: 1-1.5 g dried ginger powder per day in divided doses (studied range 0.5-2 g); motion sickness (EMA): 1-2 g powdered rhizome 30-60 min before travel. Tea: 1-2 g sliced fresh root steeped 10 min.
* '''Warnings:''' Additive bleeding risk is theoretical-to-modest with anticoagulants/antiplatelets (warfarin, clopidogrel) at >4 g/day; stop 1-2 weeks before surgery as a precaution; Heartburn, reflux and loose stool at high doses; Pregnancy: studied doses up to ~1 g/day look safe; avoid large supplemental doses near term; Gallstones: use caution (cholagogue)
* '''TCM / Ayurveda:''' TCM: fresh (sheng jiang) pungent and slightly warm; dried (gan jiang) pungent and hot. Ayurveda: 'vishwabhesaj' (universal medicine), katu rasa, ushna virya, pacifies Vata and Kapha, may aggravate Pitta.
* '''Correspondence (tradition):''' No separate Culpeper entry; listed among his simples ('Zingiberis... helps digestion, warms the stomach'). Modern Western-herbal lists assign Mars.

=== Peppermint (''Mentha x piperita'') ===
* '''Traditions:''' folk-European, Unani
* '''Used for:''' irritable bowel syndrome (enteric-coated oil); indigestion and gas; tension headache (topical oil); cold symptoms (inhalation)
* '''Compounds:''' menthol, menthone, menthyl acetate, 1,8-cineole, rosmarinic acid (leaf)
* '''Mechanism:''' Menthol blocks L-type calcium channels in intestinal smooth muscle (antispasmodic) and activates TRPM8 cold receptors; peppermint oil mildly inhibits CYP3A4 in vitro, of uncertain clinical size.
* '''Evidence:''' established. A 2019 meta-analysis of 12 RCTs (835 patients) found enteric-coated peppermint oil beat placebo for global IBS symptoms (NNT about 3) and abdominal pain (NNT about 4); EMA has a well-established-use monograph for the oil.<ref>[https://www.nccih.nih.gov/health/peppermint-oil NCCIH: Peppermint Oil]</ref><ref>[https://www.ema.europa.eu/en/medicines/herbal/menthae-piperitae-aetheroleum EMA HMPC: Menthae piperitae aetheroleum]</ref><ref>[https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6337770/ Alammar et al. 2019, The impact of peppermint oil on the irritable bowel syndrome: a meta-analysis (BMC Complement Altern Med; PMID 30654773)]</ref><ref>[https://www.gutenberg.org/ebooks/49513 Nicholas Culpeper, The Complete Herbal (Project Gutenberg eBook #49513)]</ref>
* '''Dose:''' IBS: 0.2-0.4 mL (about 180-225 mg) enteric-coated peppermint oil, 2-3 times daily before meals for up to 3 months. Tea: 1.5-3 g leaf per cup, 3 times daily. Headache: 10% oil in ethanol on temples.
* '''Warnings:''' Reflux/heartburn (relaxes lower oesophageal sphincter); non-enteric-coated oil worsens it; Do not apply oil to the face or chest of infants and young children: menthol can trigger laryngospasm/apnoea; Enteric coating dissolves early with antacids, PPIs or H2 blockers - separate by 2 h; Essential oil is toxic if swallowed neat in quantity; Gallstones/bile-duct obstruction: avoid oil
* '''TCM / Ayurveda:''' TCM (bo he, Mentha haplocalyx): pungent, cool; disperses wind-heat. Ayurveda: cooling, pacifies Pitta and Kapha.
* '''Correspondence (tradition):''' Venus (Culpeper, 'Mint: It is an herb of Venus')

=== German Chamomile (''Matricaria chamomilla (syn. M. recutita)'') ===
* '''Traditions:''' folk-European, Unani
* '''Used for:''' mild anxiety; sleep aid (folk); indigestion and colic; mouth/skin inflammation (rinse, compress)
* '''Compounds:''' apigenin, alpha-bisabolol, chamazulene (forms on distillation), matricin
* '''Mechanism:''' Apigenin binds the benzodiazepine site of GABA-A receptors weakly and inhibits COX-2 expression; bisabolol and chamazulene are anti-inflammatory; chamomile inhibits CYP1A2 and CYP3A4 in vitro.
* '''Evidence:''' traditional-with-some-evidence. Small trials suggest modest benefit for generalized anxiety disorder (oral extract) but sleep evidence is thin; EMA recognises it as a traditional herbal medicine for minor GI complaints and mouth/skin inflammation.<ref>[https://www.nccih.nih.gov/health/chamomile NCCIH: Chamomile]</ref><ref>[https://www.ema.europa.eu/en/medicines/herbal/matricariae-flos EMA HMPC: Matricariae flos]</ref><ref>[https://www.gutenberg.org/ebooks/49513 Nicholas Culpeper, The Complete Herbal (Project Gutenberg eBook #49513)]</ref>
* '''Dose:''' Tea: 2-4 g dried flower heads in 150 mL boiling water, covered 5-10 min, 3-4 times daily. Anxiety trials: 500 mg standardized extract 1-3 times daily (up to 1500 mg/day).
* '''Warnings:''' Allergy in people sensitive to Asteraceae (ragweed, daisy, marigold) - rare anaphylaxis; Possible additive bleeding with warfarin (case reports); Additive sedation with benzodiazepines, alcohol, other sedatives; Ciclosporin and other CYP3A4 substrates: monitor
* '''TCM / Ayurveda:''' Ayurveda: cooling, calms Pitta and Vata. Unani: babuna, hot and dry in first degree.
* '''Correspondence (tradition):''' Moon (Culpeper, 'Camomile... under the dominion of the Moon'); many later herbals instead give the Sun

=== Garlic (''Allium sativum'') ===
* '''Traditions:''' folk-European, TCM, Ayurveda, Unani
* '''Used for:''' modest blood-pressure lowering; modest cholesterol lowering; common cold prevention (weak); antimicrobial (folk)
* '''Compounds:''' alliin, allicin, ajoene, S-allyl cysteine (aged extract), diallyl disulfide
* '''Mechanism:''' Crushing triggers the enzyme alliinase to convert alliin to allicin within seconds (so chop and wait ~10 min before heating, which destroys alliinase); ajoene inhibits platelet aggregation, and garlic supplements lower saquinavir levels via CYP3A4/P-gp induction.
* '''Evidence:''' traditional-with-some-evidence. Meta-analyses show small BP reductions in hypertensive people and small lipid effects; the Cochrane review on preventing colds rests on a single trial and is insufficient.<ref>[https://www.nccih.nih.gov/health/garlic NCCIH: Garlic]</ref><ref>[https://www.cochrane.org/evidence/CD006206 Cochrane: Garlic for the common cold (CD006206)]</ref><ref>[https://www.gutenberg.org/ebooks/49513 Nicholas Culpeper, The Complete Herbal (Project Gutenberg eBook #49513)]</ref>
* '''Dose:''' 1 fresh clove (about 2-5 g) daily; or 600-1200 mg dried garlic powder daily in divided doses; or aged garlic extract 600-2400 mg daily.
* '''Warnings:''' Bleeding risk with warfarin/antiplatelets and before surgery (stop 7-10 days prior); Reduces blood levels of saquinavir and possibly other HIV protease inhibitors; Raw garlic on skin can cause chemical burns; Heartburn, body/breath odour
* '''TCM / Ayurveda:''' TCM (da suan): pungent, warm. Ayurveda (lasuna): five tastes except sour, hot; reduces Vata and Kapha, aggravates Pitta.
* '''Correspondence (tradition):''' Mars (Culpeper, 'Mars owns this herb... the poor man's treacle')

=== Turmeric (''Curcuma longa'') ===
* '''Traditions:''' Ayurveda, TCM, Unani
* '''Used for:''' osteoarthritis pain (modest); dyspepsia; anti-inflammatory (general claims); culinary spice
* '''Compounds:''' curcumin, demethoxycurcumin, bisdemethoxycurcumin, ar-turmerone
* '''Mechanism:''' Curcumin suppresses NF-kB signalling and COX-2/LOX expression, and inhibits CYP3A4, CYP2C9 and UGT glucuronidation; its own bioavailability is very low because it is rapidly glucuronidated - piperine (black pepper) blocks that glucuronidation and raises plasma curcumin roughly 20-fold.
* '''Evidence:''' traditional-with-some-evidence. Several small trials support knee-osteoarthritis pain relief comparable to NSAIDs, but most claims (cancer, depression, Alzheimer's) are unproven, and LiverTox now documents over a dozen cases of turmeric-supplement liver injury, especially with piperine-enhanced products.<ref>[https://www.nccih.nih.gov/health/turmeric NCCIH: Turmeric]</ref><ref>[https://www.ema.europa.eu/en/medicines/herbal/curcumae-longae-rhizoma EMA HMPC: Curcumae longae rhizoma]</ref><ref>[https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK548561/ NIH LiverTox: Turmeric (NBK548561)]</ref>
* '''Dose:''' Culinary: 1-3 g turmeric powder/day is typical dietary intake. Osteoarthritis trials: 500-2000 mg curcumin extract/day in divided doses for 8-12 weeks. EMA traditional use: 1.5-3 g dried rhizome per day.
* '''Warnings:''' Liver injury reported with concentrated supplements (LiverTox), higher risk with piperine/bioavailability-enhanced forms; Antiplatelet effect - caution with anticoagulants; CYP3A4/2C9 inhibition: may raise levels of drugs like tacrolimus, some chemotherapies; Gallstones/bile-duct obstruction: avoid (cholagogue); May lower blood sugar with diabetes drugs; iron absorption reduced
* '''TCM / Ayurveda:''' TCM (jiang huang): pungent, bitter, warm; moves blood and qi. Ayurveda (haridra): tikta and katu rasa, ushna virya; balances all three doshas, especially Kapha.

=== Honey (cough and wound) (''Mel (from Apis mellifera); medical-grade Manuka from Leptospermum scoparium nectar'') ===
* '''Traditions:''' folk-European, Ayurveda, Unani, Egyptian
* '''Used for:''' acute cough in children over 1 year; topical wound and burn dressing (medical-grade); sore throat
* '''Compounds:''' glucose oxidase (yields hydrogen peroxide), methylglyoxal (Manuka), phenolic acids and flavonoids, bee defensin-1
* '''Mechanism:''' Bee-added glucose oxidase slowly generates hydrogen peroxide when honey is diluted by wound fluid, while high sugar osmolarity and low pH inhibit bacteria; Manuka's non-peroxide activity comes from methylglyoxal (formed from nectar dihydroxyacetone). Heating destroys glucose oxidase.
* '''Evidence:''' established. Cochrane (2018, 6 RCTs, 899 children) found honey probably relieves cough symptoms better than no treatment, diphenhydramine or placebo and may be similar to dextromethorphan; for wounds, Cochrane finds honey heals partial-thickness burns faster than conventional dressings but evidence for other wounds is mixed.<ref>[https://www.cochrane.org/evidence/CD007094 Cochrane: Honey for acute cough in children (CD007094)]</ref><ref>[https://www.cochrane.org/evidence/CD005083 Cochrane: Honey as a topical treatment for acute and chronic wounds (CD005083)]</ref>
* '''Dose:''' Cough: 2.5-10 mL (1/2-2 teaspoons) at bedtime for children over 1 year (age-scaled: 1-5 y 1/2 tsp, 6-11 y 1 tsp, 12+ 2 tsp). Wounds: sterile medical-grade honey dressing changed daily or as exudate requires - not kitchen honey on deep or infected wounds.
* '''Warnings:''' NEVER give honey to infants under 12 months - risk of infant botulism (Clostridium botulinum spores); Raw kitchen honey is not sterile - use gamma-irradiated medical-grade honey on open wounds; Blood sugar: counts as sugar for diabetics; Bee/pollen allergy; 'Mad honey' from Rhododendron nectar (grayanotoxins) causes bradycardia and hypotension
* '''TCM / Ayurveda:''' Ayurveda (madhu): sweet and astringent, heating when consumed, reduces Kapha; never to be cooked or heated per classical texts. Unani: hot and dry in second degree.

=== Elderberry (''Sambucus nigra'') ===
* '''Traditions:''' folk-European
* '''Used for:''' colds and flu (folk; syrup); fever (flowers, as diaphoretic tea)
* '''Compounds:''' anthocyanins (cyanidin-3-glucoside, cyanidin-3-sambubioside), flavonols (quercetin, rutin), sambunigrin (cyanogenic glycoside, in unripe/raw parts)
* '''Mechanism:''' Anthocyanins inhibit viral neuraminidase and haemagglutination in vitro; cooking matters because raw seeds, bark, leaves and unripe berries contain sambunigrin, which the plant enzyme beta-glucosidase hydrolyses to release hydrogen cyanide.
* '''Evidence:''' traditional-with-some-evidence. Mixed: a few small, often industry-funded trials suggested shorter flu duration, but a larger 2019 RCT found no benefit in influenza; NCCIH rates evidence as insufficient.<ref>[https://www.nccih.nih.gov/health/european-elder NCCIH: European Elder (Elderberry)]</ref><ref>[https://www.ema.europa.eu/en/medicines/herbal/sambuci-fructus EMA HMPC: Sambuci fructus (elderberry)]</ref><ref>[https://www.gutenberg.org/ebooks/49513 Nicholas Culpeper, The Complete Herbal (Project Gutenberg eBook #49513)]</ref>
* '''Dose:''' Standardized syrup (e.g. Sambucol-type) studied at 15 mL four times daily for 5 days in adults; EMA traditional flower tea: 2-5 g dried flower per cup, up to 3 times daily.
* '''Warnings:''' Never eat raw berries, leaves, stems, bark or unripe fruit - cyanogenic glycosides cause vomiting, diarrhoea and in larger amounts cyanide poisoning; cook ripe berries thoroughly; Theoretical immunostimulant concern with immunosuppressants (transplant, autoimmune); Insufficient pregnancy/breast-feeding data; Mild diuretic/laxative effect
* '''Correspondence (tradition):''' Venus (Culpeper, 'Elder and Dwarf Tree are under the dominion of Venus')

=== Echinacea (purple coneflower) (''Echinacea purpurea (also E. angustifolia, E. pallida)'') ===
* '''Traditions:''' Indigenous North American, folk-European
* '''Used for:''' short-term prevention and treatment of common cold; wound healing (Plains nations, topical)
* '''Compounds:''' alkamides (dodeca-tetraenoic acid isobutylamides), caffeic acid derivatives (cichoric acid, echinacoside), polysaccharides
* '''Mechanism:''' Alkamides bind cannabinoid CB2 receptors on immune cells and modulate cytokine release; echinacea inhibits intestinal CYP3A4 but induces hepatic CYP3A4, a mixed net effect on drugs like midazolam.
* '''Evidence:''' traditional-with-some-evidence. Cochrane (24 RCTs) found products generally did not significantly beat placebo for treating colds, with a possible weak preventive effect; products vary wildly in species, part and extraction, which explains much of the inconsistency.<ref>[https://www.nccih.nih.gov/health/echinacea NCCIH: Echinacea]</ref><ref>[https://www.ema.europa.eu/en/medicines/herbal/echinaceae-purpureae-herba EMA HMPC: Echinaceae purpureae herba]</ref><ref>[https://www.cochrane.org/evidence/CD000530 Cochrane: Echinacea for preventing and treating the common cold (CD000530)]</ref>
* '''Dose:''' E. purpurea pressed juice (aerial parts): 6-9 mL daily for up to 10 days at first symptoms (EMA). Dried root/extracts: commonly 300-500 mg 3 times daily, max 10 days for treatment.
* '''Warnings:''' Asteraceae allergy - rash and rare anaphylaxis; avoid in atopic people; Theoretical conflict with immunosuppressants; EMA advises against in progressive systemic/autoimmune disease (TB, MS, HIV, collagenoses); Not for children under 12 (EMA) due to rash risk; Mixed CYP3A4 effects - monitor narrow-range drugs

=== White Willow Bark (''Salix alba (also S. purpurea, S. fragilis)'') ===
* '''Traditions:''' folk-European, TCM, Indigenous North American
* '''Used for:''' low back pain; osteoarthritis pain (mixed); fever and headache (historical)
* '''Compounds:''' salicin, salicortin, tremulacin, flavonoids, tannins
* '''Mechanism:''' Salicin is a prodrug: gut bacterial beta-glucosidases cleave it to saligenin, which the liver oxidises to salicylic acid, a weak reversible COX inhibitor - unlike aspirin it does not irreversibly acetylate platelet COX-1, so antiplatelet effect is milder and onset slower.
* '''Evidence:''' traditional-with-some-evidence. Cochrane's herbal-medicine-for-low-back-pain review found moderate evidence that willow bark extracts (120-240 mg salicin/day) reduce short-term pain better than placebo; osteoarthritis results are mixed. EMA lists it as well-established/traditional for back pain.<ref>[https://www.ema.europa.eu/en/medicines/herbal/salicis-cortex EMA HMPC: Salicis cortex (willow bark)]</ref><ref>[https://www.mskcc.org/cancer-care/integrative-medicine/herbs/willow-bark MSKCC About Herbs: Willow Bark]</ref><ref>[https://www.cochrane.org/evidence/CD004504 Cochrane: Herbal medicine for low-back pain (CD004504)]</ref><ref>[https://www.gutenberg.org/ebooks/49513 Nicholas Culpeper, The Complete Herbal (Project Gutenberg eBook #49513)]</ref>
* '''Dose:''' Extract standardized to 120-240 mg salicin per day in divided doses (EMA up to 240 mg salicin/day), for up to 4 weeks. Decoction: 1-3 g dried bark simmered 10-15 min, up to 3-4 times daily (salicin content varies by species).
* '''Warnings:''' Salicylate allergy or aspirin-induced asthma: avoid; Children/teens with viral illness: theoretical Reye's syndrome risk - avoid; Additive effect with anticoagulants, antiplatelets, NSAIDs, methotrexate; Peptic ulcer, kidney disease, G6PD deficiency: caution; Pregnancy (third trimester) and breast-feeding: avoid
* '''Correspondence (tradition):''' Moon (Culpeper, 'The Willow Tree... The Moon owns it')

=== Feverfew (''Tanacetum parthenium'') ===
* '''Traditions:''' folk-European
* '''Used for:''' migraine prevention; fever (historical); menstrual complaints (Culpeper)
* '''Compounds:''' parthenolide (sesquiterpene lactone), flavonoid glycosides, camphor
* '''Mechanism:''' Parthenolide inhibits NF-kB and IKK, blocks platelet serotonin release, and modulates TRPA1 on trigeminal nerves; it also inhibits phospholipase A2-driven prostaglandin release.
* '''Evidence:''' traditional-with-some-evidence. Cochrane (6 trials, 561 people) found only a small preventive effect - about 0.6 fewer migraines a month - with low-quality evidence; EMA lists traditional use for migraine prophylaxis.<ref>[https://www.nccih.nih.gov/health/feverfew NCCIH: Feverfew]</ref><ref>[https://www.ema.europa.eu/en/medicines/herbal/tanaceti-parthenii-herba EMA HMPC: Tanaceti parthenii herba]</ref><ref>[https://www.cochrane.org/evidence/CD002286 Cochrane: Feverfew for preventing migraine (CD002286)]</ref><ref>[https://www.gutenberg.org/ebooks/49513 Nicholas Culpeper, The Complete Herbal (Project Gutenberg eBook #49513)]</ref>
* '''Dose:''' Dried leaf powder 50-150 mg/day (often standardized to 0.2-0.4% parthenolide) taken continuously; benefit assessed after 4-6 weeks. Folk practice: 2-3 fresh leaves daily (chewing causes mouth ulcers in some).
* '''Warnings:''' Pregnancy: avoid (emmenagogue; historical abortifacient); Asteraceae allergy; Antiplatelet effect - caution with anticoagulants; 'Post-feverfew syndrome' on abrupt stop: rebound headache, anxiety, joint stiffness - taper; Mouth ulcers and tongue swelling from chewing fresh leaves
* '''Correspondence (tradition):''' Venus (Culpeper, 'Venus commands this herb... to succour her sisters (women)')

=== Valerian (''Valeriana officinalis'') ===
* '''Traditions:''' folk-European, Ayurveda (tagara, V. wallichii)
* '''Used for:''' insomnia; nervous tension; mild anxiety
* '''Compounds:''' valerenic acid, valepotriates (valtrate), isovaleric acid (the smell), hesperidin/linarin
* '''Mechanism:''' Valerenic acid positively modulates GABA-A receptors containing beta2/beta3 subunits and inhibits GABA transaminase (the enzyme that breaks down GABA); in humans CYP effects are minor (no meaningful CYP3A4/2D6 change at normal doses).
* '''Evidence:''' traditional-with-some-evidence. Systematic reviews are inconsistent: some subjective sleep-quality improvement but objective sleep measures rarely change; EMA nonetheless grants well-established use for the ethanolic root extract.<ref>[https://www.nccih.nih.gov/health/valerian NCCIH: Valerian]</ref><ref>[https://www.ema.europa.eu/en/medicines/herbal/valerianae-radix EMA HMPC: Valerianae radix]</ref><ref>[https://www.gutenberg.org/ebooks/49513 Nicholas Culpeper, The Complete Herbal (Project Gutenberg eBook #49513)]</ref>
* '''Dose:''' 300-600 mg root extract (or 2-3 g dried root as tea) 30 min-2 h before bed; effects build over 2-4 weeks.
* '''Warnings:''' Additive sedation with alcohol, benzodiazepines, barbiturates, opioids, other sedatives; Do not drive if drowsy; Rare liver injury reports (often multi-herb products); Paradoxical stimulation/headache in some; Taper after long use; not for under-12s (EMA)
* '''TCM / Ayurveda:''' Ayurveda (tagara): bitter, pungent, heating; pacifies Vata and Kapha.
* '''Correspondence (tradition):''' Mercury (Culpeper, 'Garden Valerian... under the influence of Mercury')

=== Lavender (''Lavandula angustifolia'') ===
* '''Traditions:''' folk-European, Unani
* '''Used for:''' anxiety (oral oil capsules); sleep (aromatherapy); minor burns and insect bites (folk)
* '''Compounds:''' linalool, linalyl acetate, 1,8-cineole, camphor (low in L. angustifolia)
* '''Mechanism:''' Linalool and linalyl acetate inhibit voltage-gated calcium channels and modulate GABA-A transmission; the standardized oral oil Silexan reduces serotonin-1A-related anxiety without benzodiazepine-like dependence.
* '''Evidence:''' traditional-with-some-evidence. Several RCTs of oral lavender oil (Silexan, 80-160 mg/day) show anxiety reduction similar to low-dose lorazepam or paroxetine in some trials; aromatherapy evidence is weaker and hard to blind.<ref>[https://www.nccih.nih.gov/health/lavender NCCIH: Lavender]</ref><ref>[https://www.ema.europa.eu/en/medicines/herbal/lavandulae-flos EMA HMPC: Lavandulae flos]</ref><ref>[https://www.gutenberg.org/ebooks/49513 Nicholas Culpeper, The Complete Herbal (Project Gutenberg eBook #49513)]</ref>
* '''Dose:''' Anxiety: 80-160 mg standardized oral lavender oil (Silexan) once daily. Tea: 1-2 tsp dried flower per cup. Aromatherapy: 2-4 drops in diffuser. Topical: dilute 1-2% in carrier oil.
* '''Warnings:''' Additive sedation with CNS depressants; Oral capsules: burping, GI upset; Possible link between topical lavender/tea-tree products and prepubertal gynecomastia in boys (case series; disputed); Contact dermatitis, especially oxidised oil; Essential oil should not be swallowed except as a formulated capsule
* '''TCM / Ayurveda:''' Unani (ustukhudus): hot and dry, a 'brain-cleanser'.
* '''Correspondence (tradition):''' Mercury (Culpeper, 'Mercury owns the herb; and it carries his effects very potently')

=== St John's Wort (''Hypericum perforatum'') ===
* '''Traditions:''' folk-European
* '''Used for:''' mild to moderate depression; nerve pain (topical oil, folk); wound healing (red oil, folk)
* '''Compounds:''' hyperforin, hypericin, pseudohypericin, flavonoids (quercetin, hyperoside)
* '''Mechanism:''' Hyperforin is one of the most potent known natural agonists of the pregnane X receptor (PXR), strongly inducing CYP3A4, CYP2C9, CYP2C19 and P-glycoprotein; it also broadly inhibits reuptake of serotonin, noradrenaline and dopamine by raising intracellular sodium.
* '''Evidence:''' established. Cochrane (29 trials, 5489 patients) found standardized extracts better than placebo and similar to standard antidepressants for mild-to-moderate major depression, with fewer side effects; EMA grants well-established use.<ref>[https://www.nccih.nih.gov/health/st-johns-wort NCCIH: St. John's Wort]</ref><ref>[https://www.ema.europa.eu/en/medicines/herbal/hyperici-herba-0 EMA HMPC: Hyperici herba (St John's wort)]</ref><ref>[https://www.cochrane.org/evidence/CD000448 Cochrane: St John's wort for treating depression (CD000448)]</ref><ref>[https://www.gutenberg.org/ebooks/49513 Nicholas Culpeper, The Complete Herbal (Project Gutenberg eBook #49513)]</ref>
* '''Dose:''' 300 mg extract (standardized to 0.3% hypericin and/or 3-5% hyperforin) three times daily (900 mg/day); allow 4-6 weeks.
* '''Warnings:''' MAJOR interactions via CYP3A4/P-gp induction: can cause failure of oral contraceptives (breakthrough pregnancy), transplant rejection (ciclosporin, tacrolimus), HIV treatment failure (protease inhibitors, NNRTIs), reduced warfarin, digoxin, irinotecan, imatinib, some statins and opioids; Serotonin syndrome with SSRIs, SNRIs, triptans, tramadol, MAOIs - do not combine; Photosensitivity (hypericin), especially fair skin or with UV therapy; Can trigger mania in bipolar disorder; Induction persists ~2 weeks after stopping
* '''Correspondence (tradition):''' Sun, in Leo (Culpeper, 'under the celestial sign Leo, and the dominion of the Sun')

=== Cranberry (''Vaccinium macrocarpon'') ===
* '''Traditions:''' Indigenous North American, folk-European
* '''Used for:''' prevention of recurrent urinary tract infection
* '''Compounds:''' A-type proanthocyanidins (PACs), quercetin, ursolic acid, hippuric acid precursors
* '''Mechanism:''' A-type proanthocyanidins block P-fimbriae adhesion of uropathogenic E. coli to bladder epithelium (anti-adhesion, not urine acidification); cranberry is a weak CYP2C9 inhibitor at most.
* '''Evidence:''' established. The 2023 Cochrane update (50 trials, 8857 people) concluded cranberry products reduce the risk of symptomatic UTI in women with recurrent UTIs, children, and after interventions - but not in elderly institutionalised people, pregnant women or people with neurogenic bladder. It does not treat an active infection.<ref>[https://www.nccih.nih.gov/health/cranberry NCCIH: Cranberry]</ref><ref>[https://www.cochrane.org/evidence/CD001321 Cochrane: Cranberries for preventing urinary tract infections (CD001321)]</ref><ref>[https://www.gutenberg.org/ebooks/49513 Nicholas Culpeper, The Complete Herbal (Project Gutenberg eBook #49513)]</ref>
* '''Dose:''' Prevention: products delivering about 36 mg PACs (DMAC/BL-DMAC method) daily, e.g. 240-300 mL 27% juice cocktail or standardized capsules (often 500 mg twice daily).
* '''Warnings:''' Not a treatment for active UTI or kidney infection - fever/flank pain needs antibiotics; Warfarin: case reports of raised INR; trials show small effect - monitor; Large amounts may raise oxalate kidney-stone risk; Juice cocktails are high in sugar
* '''Correspondence (tradition):''' Culpeper has no cranberry entry; his related whortleberries are given to Jupiter

=== Fennel (''Foeniculum vulgare'') ===
* '''Traditions:''' folk-European, Ayurveda, Unani, TCM
* '''Used for:''' bloating and wind; infant colic (folk); menstrual cramps; lactation (folk, galactagogue)
* '''Compounds:''' trans-anethole, fenchone, estragole, limonene
* '''Mechanism:''' Anethole relaxes gut smooth muscle and has weak oestrogen-like activity; estragole is bioactivated by CYP1A2/2A6 to 1'-hydroxyestragole and then by sulfotransferase (SULT1A1) to a DNA-reactive ester - the reason EMA restricts long-term and child use.
* '''Evidence:''' traditional-with-some-evidence. Small trials suggest benefit for infant colic and dysmenorrhoea but are low-quality; EMA approves traditional use for mild spasmodic GI complaints.<ref>[https://www.ema.europa.eu/en/medicines/herbal/foeniculi-amari-fructus EMA HMPC: Foeniculi amari fructus (bitter fennel)]</ref><ref>[https://www.gutenberg.org/ebooks/49513 Nicholas Culpeper, The Complete Herbal (Project Gutenberg eBook #49513)]</ref>
* '''Dose:''' Adults: 1.5-2.5 g crushed seed infused as tea, 3 times daily (crush just before use). Do not exceed 2 weeks continuous use.
* '''Warnings:''' EMA: not recommended under 4 years and in pregnancy/breast-feeding because of estragole; avoid concentrated fennel oil; Celery/carrot/mugwort (Apiaceae) cross-allergy; Oestrogen-like activity: caution in hormone-sensitive cancers; Ciprofloxacin absorption reduced (animal data) - separate doses
* '''TCM / Ayurveda:''' Ayurveda (shatapushpa/saunf): sweet, cooling; balances all doshas, especially Pitta and Vata. Unani (badiyan): hot and dry in second degree. TCM (xiao hui xiang): pungent, warm.
* '''Correspondence (tradition):''' Mercury, in Virgo (Culpeper, 'an herb of Mercury')

=== Clove (''Syzygium aromaticum'') ===
* '''Traditions:''' Ayurveda, TCM, Unani, folk-European
* '''Used for:''' toothache and dental pain (topical oil); mouth infections; digestive warmth (culinary)
* '''Compounds:''' eugenol (70-90% of oil), beta-caryophyllene, eugenyl acetate
* '''Mechanism:''' Eugenol blocks voltage-gated sodium channels and activates/desensitises TRPV1 (local anaesthetic), inhibits COX-2, and inhibits platelet thromboxane synthesis; beta-caryophyllene is a CB2 agonist.
* '''Evidence:''' traditional-with-some-evidence. Eugenol is an established dental material (zinc oxide-eugenol dressings) and EMA lists clove oil for traditional temporary relief of dental pain; systemic claims are untested.<ref>[https://www.ema.europa.eu/en/medicines/herbal/caryophylli-floris-aetheroleum EMA HMPC: Caryophylli floris aetheroleum (clove oil)]</ref><ref>[https://www.gutenberg.org/ebooks/49513 Nicholas Culpeper, The Complete Herbal (Project Gutenberg eBook #49513)]</ref>
* '''Dose:''' Toothache: 1 drop clove oil on a cotton pellet applied to the cavity/affected area, up to 3 times daily for a few days (EMA). Culinary: whole/ground clove in food.
* '''Warnings:''' Undiluted oil can burn gums, mucosa and skin; Swallowing clove oil is dangerous in children: as little as 5-10 mL has caused liver failure, seizures and coma; Antiplatelet - caution with anticoagulants and before surgery; Not for dental abscess - see a dentist
* '''TCM / Ayurveda:''' TCM (ding xiang): pungent, warm; warms the middle and descends rebellious qi. Ayurveda (lavanga): katu and tikta rasa, cooling virya per some texts; reduces Kapha and Pitta. Unani (qaranful): hot and dry in third degree.
* '''Correspondence (tradition):''' Culpeper's 'clove gilliflowers' are carnations, not the spice; no traditional Culpeper ruler for clove. Modern lists assign Jupiter.

=== Aloe vera (''Aloe barbadensis Miller (syn. Aloe vera)'') ===
* '''Traditions:''' Ayurveda, TCM, Unani, Egyptian, folk-European
* '''Used for:''' minor burns and sunburn (gel); skin irritation; constipation (latex - now discouraged)
* '''Compounds:''' acemannan (gel polysaccharide), aloin/barbaloin (latex anthraquinone), aloe-emodin, bradykinase-type carboxypeptidase
* '''Mechanism:''' The inner gel contains a carboxypeptidase that degrades bradykinin (the 'bradykinase' anti-inflammatory activity) plus acemannan that stimulates fibroblasts; the yellow latex aloin is a prodrug cleaved by gut bacterial beta-glucosidases to aloe-emodin anthrone, a stimulant laxative.
* '''Evidence:''' traditional-with-some-evidence. Topical gel has some evidence for burns and psoriasis but results are mixed; oral latex laxatives were withdrawn from US OTC sale in 2002 over lack of safety data, and whole-leaf extract caused intestinal tumours in rats.<ref>[https://www.nccih.nih.gov/health/aloe-vera NCCIH: Aloe Vera]</ref>
* '''Dose:''' Topical: apply fresh or commercial gel (inner leaf only) to the affected skin 2-3 times daily. Oral gel juice: products decolourised to <10 ppm aloin, commonly 30-60 mL/day; avoid latex.
* '''Warnings:''' Oral latex: cramping, diarrhoea, potassium loss - dangerous with digoxin, diuretics, corticosteroids; Oral aloe: case reports of acute hepatitis; May lower blood sugar - monitor on diabetes drugs; Pregnancy: oral latex can stimulate uterine contractions - avoid; Do not apply to deep or surgical wounds (one trial showed delayed healing)
* '''TCM / Ayurveda:''' Ayurveda (kumari/ghritkumari): bitter, sweet, cooling; pacifies Pitta and Kapha. TCM (lu hui, the dried latex): bitter, cold; purges heat.

=== Asian ginseng (''Panax ginseng'') ===
* '''Traditions:''' TCM, Korean traditional medicine
* '''Used for:''' fatigue and stamina (adaptogen); erectile dysfunction (some evidence); blood-sugar modulation; cognition (claimed)
* '''Compounds:''' ginsenosides (Rb1, Rg1, Rg3, Re), polysaccharides, polyacetylenes
* '''Mechanism:''' Ginsenosides are glycosides that gut bacteria de-glycosylate to active metabolites (e.g. Rb1 to compound K); ginseng increases nitric oxide synthase activity in vascular/erectile tissue and may induce CYP3A4 modestly in humans.
* '''Evidence:''' traditional-with-some-evidence. Some trials support erectile-function improvement and modest glucose lowering, but Cochrane found no convincing evidence of cognitive enhancement, and fatigue data are mixed.<ref>[https://www.nccih.nih.gov/health/asian-ginseng NCCIH: Asian Ginseng]</ref><ref>[https://www.ema.europa.eu/en/medicines/herbal/ginseng-radix EMA HMPC: Ginseng radix]</ref><ref>[https://www.cochrane.org/evidence/CD007769 Cochrane: Panax ginseng for cognition (CD007769)]</ref>
* '''Dose:''' 200-400 mg standardized extract (4-7% ginsenosides) daily, or 1-2 g dried root daily; traditionally cycled (e.g. 2-3 weeks on, 1-2 weeks off). Red ginseng for ED trials: 900 mg 3 times daily.
* '''Warnings:''' Warfarin: reduced INR reported (ginseng lowered warfarin effect in a trial) - monitor; Insomnia, nervousness, headache; avoid with stimulants; May lower blood sugar - hypoglycaemia risk with insulin/sulfonylureas; Interaction reports with MAOI phenelzine (mania, headache); Hypertension: caution at high doses ('ginseng abuse syndrome'); pregnancy: avoid (ginsenoside Rb1 teratogenic in animal embryos)
* '''TCM / Ayurveda:''' TCM (ren shen): sweet, slightly bitter, slightly warm (red ginseng warmer); greatly tonifies yuan qi, enters Spleen and Lung.

=== Ashwagandha (''Withania somnifera'') ===
* '''Traditions:''' Ayurveda, Unani
* '''Used for:''' stress and anxiety; sleep; rasayana (rejuvenative) tonic; male fertility/testosterone (small trials)
* '''Compounds:''' withanolides (withaferin A, withanolide A, withanone), sitoindosides, alkaloids (tropine, anaferine)
* '''Mechanism:''' Withanolides act as GABA-mimetics and lower cortisol by damping HPA-axis activity; withaferin A inhibits NF-kB and the proteasome; ashwagandha may raise thyroid hormone (T4) levels.
* '''Evidence:''' traditional-with-some-evidence. Multiple small RCTs (mostly from India, 8-12 weeks) show reduced perceived stress and cortisol, but certainty is low; LiverTox rates it a 'likely cause' (B) of clinically apparent liver injury, including rare fatal cases.<ref>[https://www.nccih.nih.gov/health/ashwagandha NCCIH: Ashwagandha]</ref><ref>[https://ods.od.nih.gov/factsheets/Ashwagandha-HealthProfessional/ NIH Office of Dietary Supplements: Ashwagandha - Health Professional Fact Sheet]</ref><ref>[https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK548536/ NIH LiverTox: Ashwagandha (NBK548536)]</ref>
* '''Dose:''' Root extract 250-600 mg/day (e.g. KSM-66 300 mg twice daily) for 8-12 weeks; traditional churna 3-6 g root powder in warm milk at night.
* '''Warnings:''' Liver injury (cholestatic, 2-12 weeks after starting) - stop if jaundice, itching, dark urine; avoid with liver disease; Pregnancy: avoid (traditional abortifacient at high doses); Thyroid: may raise T4 - caution with hyperthyroidism or levothyroxine; Additive sedation with benzodiazepines, alcohol; Immunosuppressants and autoimmune disease: theoretical immunostimulation; nightshade family allergy
* '''TCM / Ayurveda:''' Ayurveda: tikta, kashaya and madhura rasa, ushna virya; pacifies Vata and Kapha, may aggravate Pitta/ama in excess.

=== Holy Basil (Tulsi) (''Ocimum tenuiflorum (syn. O. sanctum)'') ===
* '''Traditions:''' Ayurveda, Hindu devotional
* '''Used for:''' stress (adaptogen); cough and colds (tea); blood sugar; oral health
* '''Compounds:''' eugenol, ursolic acid, rosmarinic acid, beta-caryophyllene, methyl eugenol
* '''Mechanism:''' Eugenol and ursolic acid inhibit COX-2; tulsi extracts lower cortisol in small trials and inhibit CYP enzymes (CYP2C9, CYP3A4) in vitro; it is the sacred plant of Vishnu/Lakshmi, grown in a tulsi vrindavan at Hindu homes.
* '''Evidence:''' traditional-with-some-evidence. MSKCC summarises small clinical studies suggesting reduced stress, anxiety and improved sleep and metabolic markers, but trials are short, small and heterogeneous.<ref>[https://www.mskcc.org/cancer-care/integrative-medicine/herbs/holy-basil-01 MSKCC About Herbs: Holy Basil]</ref>
* '''Dose:''' Tea: 1-2 tsp dried leaf (or 5-10 fresh leaves) per cup, 1-3 times daily. Trials: 300 mg-1 g leaf extract daily for 4-8 weeks.
* '''Warnings:''' May lower blood sugar - hypoglycaemia with diabetes drugs; Antiplatelet effect - caution with anticoagulants, before surgery; Pregnancy/conception: animal data show anti-fertility effects - avoid if trying to conceive; Contains methyl eugenol (a rodent carcinogen in isolated form) - favour moderate tea use over concentrated oils
* '''TCM / Ayurveda:''' Ayurveda: katu and tikta rasa, ushna virya; pacifies Kapha and Vata, increases Pitta.
* '''Correspondence (tradition):''' Culpeper's 'Garden Basil' (O. basilicum, a different species) is given to Mars

=== Triphala (with Amla) (''Phyllanthus emblica (amla) + Terminalia chebula (haritaki) + Terminalia bellirica (bibhitaki)'') ===
* '''Traditions:''' Ayurveda, Unani (itrifal)
* '''Used for:''' constipation (gentle laxative); digestive tonic; oral/gum health (rinse); rasayana; amla as vitamin C-rich fruit
* '''Compounds:''' gallic acid, chebulagic and chebulinic acids, ellagitannins (emblicanins), ascorbic acid (amla)
* '''Mechanism:''' Hydrolysable tannins (chebulinic, gallic acids) inhibit alpha-glucosidase and alpha-amylase and are antioxidants; anthraquinone-type glycosides in haritaki are hydrolysed by gut bacteria to mild laxative aglycones; triphala inhibits CYP3A4 and CYP2D6 in vitro.
* '''Evidence:''' traditional-with-some-evidence. Small trials support a mild laxative effect and plaque/gingivitis reduction as a mouthwash; amla trials show modest lipid and glucose improvements; large rigorous trials are lacking.<ref>[https://www.mskcc.org/cancer-care/integrative-medicine/herbs/triphala MSKCC About Herbs: Triphala]</ref>
* '''Dose:''' Triphala churna 3-5 g (about 1 tsp) in warm water at bedtime, or 500-1000 mg tablets 1-2 times daily. Amla: 1-3 g dried fruit powder daily or one fresh fruit.
* '''Warnings:''' Diarrhoea and cramping at higher doses; avoid with active diarrhoea; Pregnancy: avoid (haritaki traditionally contraindicated); May potentiate diabetes drugs and anticoagulants (amla antiplatelet effect); Heavy-metal contamination has been found in some Ayurvedic products - buy tested brands; In-vitro CYP inhibition - caution with narrow-range drugs
* '''TCM / Ayurveda:''' Ayurveda: tridoshic - amla balances Pitta, haritaki Vata, bibhitaki Kapha; together five tastes except salty.

=== Licorice root (''Glycyrrhiza glabra (also G. uralensis in TCM)'') ===
* '''Traditions:''' folk-European, TCM, Ayurveda, Unani, Egyptian
* '''Used for:''' sore throat and cough (demulcent); dyspepsia and peptic ulcer (DGL); TCM formula harmonizer
* '''Compounds:''' glycyrrhizin (glycyrrhizic acid), glycyrrhetinic acid, liquiritigenin, glabridin, isoliquiritigenin
* '''Mechanism:''' Glycyrrhizin is hydrolysed by gut bacteria to glycyrrhetinic acid, which inhibits 11-beta-hydroxysteroid dehydrogenase type 2 in the kidney so cortisol over-activates mineralocorticoid receptors - causing sodium retention, potassium loss and high blood pressure (pseudo-aldosteronism); deglycyrrhizinated licorice (DGL) removes this.
* '''Evidence:''' traditional-with-some-evidence. EMA accepts traditional use for cough and dyspepsia; DGL ulcer evidence is old and limited; the mineralocorticoid toxicity is well established. LiverTox notes no clinically apparent liver injury.<ref>[https://www.nccih.nih.gov/health/licorice-root NCCIH: Licorice Root]</ref><ref>[https://www.ema.europa.eu/en/medicines/herbal/liquiritiae-radix EMA HMPC: Liquiritiae radix]</ref><ref>[https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK590484/ NIH LiverTox: Licorice (NBK590484)]</ref><ref>[https://www.gutenberg.org/ebooks/49513 Nicholas Culpeper, The Complete Herbal (Project Gutenberg eBook #49513)]</ref>
* '''Dose:''' Cough/dyspepsia: 1.5-5 g dried root as decoction daily (EMA), keeping glycyrrhizin below about 100 mg/day and for no more than 4-6 weeks. DGL: 380-760 mg chewed 20 min before meals.
* '''Warnings:''' Hypertension, oedema, hypokalaemia (low potassium) and arrhythmia with regular intake above ~100 mg glycyrrhizin/day (about 50 g black licorice candy) - FDA has warned adults over 40; Dangerous with diuretics, digoxin (hypokalaemia), corticosteroids, antihypertensives; Avoid in heart failure, kidney disease, hypertension; Pregnancy: heavy use linked to preterm birth and later cognitive effects - avoid; Inhibits CYP3A4 (glabridin) in vitro
* '''TCM / Ayurveda:''' TCM (gan cao): sweet, neutral; harmonizes all herbs in a formula, tonifies Spleen qi, moistens Lung. Ayurveda (yashtimadhu): madhura rasa, sheeta virya; pacifies Vata and Pitta.
* '''Correspondence (tradition):''' Mercury (Culpeper, 'Liquorice... under the dominion of Mercury')

=== Astragalus (Huang Qi) (''Astragalus membranaceus (syn. A. mongholicus)'') ===
* '''Traditions:''' TCM
* '''Used for:''' qi tonic for fatigue; immune support (colds); adjunct in chemotherapy and kidney disease (TCM practice)
* '''Compounds:''' astragalosides (astragaloside IV), cycloastragenol, polysaccharides, isoflavones (formononetin, calycosin)
* '''Mechanism:''' Cycloastragenol is reported to activate telomerase in cell studies (the basis of anti-ageing marketing - unproven in humans); polysaccharides stimulate macrophage and T-cell cytokine release.
* '''Evidence:''' traditional-only. NCCIH rates human evidence as insufficient; many positive trials are small, Chinese-language, and of low methodological quality.<ref>[https://www.nccih.nih.gov/health/astragalus NCCIH: Astragalus]</ref>
* '''Dose:''' 9-30 g dried root per day decocted (TCM standard range), or 500 mg-1 g extract 2-3 times daily.
* '''Warnings:''' Immunosuppressants (ciclosporin, tacrolimus) and autoimmune disease: theoretical opposition; May interact with lithium (diuretic effect may raise levels); Some Astragalus species (locoweeds, not A. membranaceus) are toxic - buy correct species; Insufficient pregnancy data
* '''TCM / Ayurveda:''' TCM: sweet, slightly warm; tonifies Spleen and Lung qi, raises yang, consolidates wei qi (exterior).

=== Ginkgo (''Ginkgo biloba'') ===
* '''Traditions:''' TCM, modern European phytotherapy
* '''Used for:''' memory and dementia (claimed); intermittent claudication; tinnitus (claimed)
* '''Compounds:''' flavone glycosides (quercetin, kaempferol), terpene lactones (ginkgolides A/B/C, bilobalide), ginkgolic acids (allergenic, removed in EGb 761)
* '''Mechanism:''' Ginkgolide B antagonises platelet-activating factor (PAF) receptors; ginkgo induces CYP2C19 (lowers omeprazole levels) and has variable CYP3A4 effects.
* '''Evidence:''' traditional-with-some-evidence. Cochrane found no convincing evidence that ginkgo works for dementia or cognitive impairment, and the large GEM trial found no prevention of dementia; modest evidence for claudication walking distance.<ref>[https://www.nccih.nih.gov/health/ginkgo NCCIH: Ginkgo]</ref><ref>[https://www.ema.europa.eu/en/medicines/herbal/ginkgo-folium EMA HMPC: Ginkgo folium]</ref><ref>[https://www.cochrane.org/evidence/CD003120 Cochrane: Ginkgo biloba for cognitive impairment and dementia (CD003120)]</ref>
* '''Dose:''' 120-240 mg/day standardized leaf extract (EGb 761: 24% flavone glycosides, 6% terpene lactones) in 2-3 divided doses.
* '''Warnings:''' Bleeding: case reports of intracranial haemorrhage; caution with warfarin, aspirin, clopidogrel, NSAIDs; stop 36 h-2 weeks before surgery; Seeds (raw or many roasted) contain ginkgotoxin (4'-O-methylpyridoxine), an anti-vitamin B6 that causes seizures; Seizure threshold: caution with epilepsy; Lowers omeprazole and possibly efavirenz levels (CYP2C19/3A4); Raw leaf/tea contains allergenic ginkgolic acids
* '''TCM / Ayurveda:''' TCM (bai guo = seed; yin xing ye = leaf): seed sweet, bitter, astringent, neutral, slightly toxic; stabilises Lung qi and stops wheezing.

=== Black Seed (Habbatus Sauda) (''Nigella sativa'') ===
* '''Traditions:''' Unani, Ayurveda (kalonji), Islamic Prophetic medicine (Tibb al-Nabawi), Egyptian
* '''Used for:''' blood sugar (type 2 diabetes adjunct); blood pressure and lipids; asthma and allergy (small trials); general tonic
* '''Compounds:''' thymoquinone, thymohydroquinone, dithymoquinone, nigellone, alpha-hederin
* '''Mechanism:''' Thymoquinone inhibits 5-LOX and COX (leukotriene and prostaglandin reduction) and NF-kB, and inhibits CYP2C9 and CYP3A4 in vitro and in animal models.
* '''Evidence:''' traditional-with-some-evidence. A 2022 systematic review of 17 clinical studies found consistent modest HbA1c and glucose reductions, and smaller trials show lipid and BP effects; most trials are small, short and use uncharacterised products. Seeds were found in Tutankhamun's tomb, and a hadith calls it 'a cure for every disease except death'.<ref>[https://www.mskcc.org/cancer-care/integrative-medicine/herbs/nigella-sativa MSKCC About Herbs: Nigella sativa (black seed)]</ref><ref>[https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC9602931/ Nigella sativa L. and its active compound thymoquinone in the clinical management of diabetes: a systematic review (Int J Mol Sci 2022)]</ref><ref>[https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5633670/ Review of randomized clinical trials of Nigella sativa and thymoquinone (J Pharmacopuncture 2017)]</ref>
* '''Dose:''' Ground seed 1-3 g/day (diabetes trials often 2 g/day), or seed oil 1-3 mL (about 1 tsp) daily, for 8-12 weeks.
* '''Warnings:''' May lower blood sugar and blood pressure - additive with diabetes and BP drugs; Antiplatelet effect - caution with anticoagulants; Topical oil: allergic contact dermatitis reported; Pregnancy: high doses inhibit uterine contraction in animal studies - avoid medicinal doses; Case reports of acute kidney injury at high doses; CYP2C9/3A4 inhibition (e.g. with warfarin, cyclosporine)
* '''TCM / Ayurveda:''' Unani (shuneez/kalonji): hot and dry in third degree. Ayurveda (krishna jiraka/upakunchika): katu and tikta rasa, ushna virya; pacifies Kapha and Vata.

=== Sage (with note on Rosemary) (''Salvia officinalis (rosemary: Salvia rosmarinus, syn. Rosmarinus officinalis)'') ===
* '''Traditions:''' folk-European, Unani
* '''Used for:''' sore throat and mouth inflammation (gargle); excessive sweating and hot flushes; memory (small trials); rosemary: digestive complaints and circulation (EMA)
* '''Compounds:''' thujone (alpha/beta), camphor, 1,8-cineole, rosmarinic acid, carnosic acid/carnosol
* '''Mechanism:''' Sage inhibits acetylcholinesterase and butyrylcholinesterase (the basis of the cholinergic memory trials); thujone is a GABA-A antagonist, which is why concentrated oils are convulsant; carnosic acid in both sage and rosemary is a potent lipid antioxidant (Nrf2 activator).
* '''Evidence:''' traditional-with-some-evidence. Small RCTs show sage improves menopausal hot flushes and short-term memory in healthy and mild-Alzheimer's subjects, and EMA accepts traditional use for sweating and throat inflammation; rosemary's cognitive claims rest on very small studies.<ref>[https://www.nccih.nih.gov/health/sage NCCIH: Sage]</ref><ref>[https://www.ema.europa.eu/en/medicines/herbal/salviae-officinalis-folium EMA HMPC: Salviae officinalis folium]</ref><ref>[https://www.ema.europa.eu/en/medicines/herbal/rosmarini-folium EMA HMPC: Rosmarini folium]</ref><ref>[https://www.gutenberg.org/ebooks/49513 Nicholas Culpeper, The Complete Herbal (Project Gutenberg eBook #49513)]</ref>
* '''Dose:''' Gargle: 2-3 g dried leaf in 150 mL water, several times daily. Hot flushes/sweating: 1-2 g leaf as tea up to 3 times daily or 300 mg extract daily. Limit to 2 weeks for internal use (EMA) because of thujone. Rosemary tea: 4-6 g leaf/day (EMA).
* '''Warnings:''' Sage essential oil / concentrated extracts can cause seizures (thujone) - never ingest the oil; avoid in epilepsy; Pregnancy and breast-feeding: avoid medicinal doses (thujone; sage dries milk); May lower blood sugar; anticholinergic/cholinergic drug interactions possible; Rosemary: large amounts may be uterotonic in pregnancy; oil is convulsant in excess
* '''TCM / Ayurveda:''' Unani (sage, salbia): hot and dry.
* '''Correspondence (tradition):''' Sage: Jupiter (Culpeper, 'Jupiter claims this... good for the liver, and to breed blood'); Rosemary: Sun, in Aries (Culpeper, 'The Sun claims privilege in it, and it is under the celestial Ram')

=== Fenugreek (''Trigonella foenum-graecum'') ===
* '''Traditions:''' Ayurveda, Unani, TCM, Egyptian, folk-European
* '''Used for:''' blood sugar (type 2 diabetes adjunct); breast-milk supply (folk galactagogue); loss of appetite; topical poultice for boils/inflammation (EMA, Culpeper)
* '''Compounds:''' 4-hydroxyisoleucine, galactomannan fibre, diosgenin (steroidal saponin), trigonelline, sotolon (maple-syrup odour)
* '''Mechanism:''' Galactomannan fibre slows carbohydrate absorption and 4-hydroxyisoleucine stimulates glucose-dependent insulin secretion; extracts inhibit intestinal alpha-amylase and alpha-glucosidase.
* '''Evidence:''' traditional-with-some-evidence. Meta-analyses show modest fasting glucose and HbA1c reductions; evidence for increasing breast milk is weak and inconsistent. EMA accepts traditional use for appetite loss and topically for minor inflammation.<ref>[https://www.nccih.nih.gov/health/fenugreek NCCIH: Fenugreek]</ref><ref>[https://www.ema.europa.eu/en/medicines/herbal/trigonellae-foenugraeci-semen EMA HMPC: Trigonellae foenugraeci semen]</ref><ref>[https://www.gutenberg.org/ebooks/49513 Nicholas Culpeper, The Complete Herbal (Project Gutenberg eBook #49513)]</ref>
* '''Dose:''' Diabetes trials: 5-25 g seed powder daily with meals (often 10 g soaked seed), or 1 g hydroalcoholic extract daily. EMA appetite: 1-6 g seed per day. Topical poultice: 50 g powdered seed in 250 mL water.
* '''Warnings:''' Hypoglycaemia with insulin and diabetes drugs - monitor glucose; May enhance warfarin effect (case reports); Pregnancy: uterine stimulant - avoid medicinal doses; Peanut/chickpea (legume) cross-allergy; Maple-syrup odour of sweat and urine (can mimic maple-syrup urine disease in newborns of nursing mothers); Fibre can reduce absorption of oral drugs - separate by 2 h
* '''TCM / Ayurveda:''' Ayurveda (methi): katu and tikta rasa, ushna virya; pacifies Vata and Kapha, can raise Pitta. Unani (hulba): hot and dry in second degree. TCM (hu lu ba): bitter, warm; warms kidney yang.
* '''Correspondence (tradition):''' No Culpeper entry of its own (used as an ingredient in his poultices); modern lists assign Mercury

== Gemstones ==
=== Amethyst ===
* '''Mineral:''' Quartz, SiO2 (trigonal tectosilicate); purple colour from Fe3+ colour centres activated by natural irradiation; Mohs 7.
* '''Tradition:''' Greek amethystos = 'not intoxicated' - worn or used as a drinking vessel against drunkenness; associated with Bacchus/Dionysus myth (Renaissance retelling); modern New-Age: crown chakra, Jupiter/Neptune, Pisces and Aquarius; February birthstone; bishops' rings in Christian tradition.
* '''History:''' Amethyst was carved into beads and amulets in Predynastic and Middle Kingdom Egypt (mined at Wadi el-Hudi) and was among the 'cardinal gems' ranked with diamond and ruby until large Brazilian deposits made it common in the 19th century.<ref>[https://www.gia.edu/amethyst GIA: Amethyst]</ref>
* '''Evidence:''' tradition-only (no clinical evidence for healing claims)
* '''Safety:''' Chemically inert and insoluble; safe to handle and in water. Colour fades with prolonged sunlight or heat.

=== Rose Quartz ===
* '''Mineral:''' Quartz, SiO2; pink colour mostly from microscopic fibrous inclusions of a dumortierite-related borosilicate; usually massive, cloudy; Mohs 7.
* '''Tradition:''' Modern New-Age: heart chakra, Venus, Taurus and Libra, 'stone of love'; ancient-use claims (Egyptian face masks, Eros myth) circulate online but are not well documented.
* '''History:''' Rose quartz was carved into snuff bottles, vessels and figures in Qing-dynasty China and became a popular bead and cabochon material worldwide from the 19th-20th centuries.<ref>[https://www.gia.edu/rose-quartz GIA: Rose Quartz]</ref>
* '''Evidence:''' tradition-only (no clinical evidence for healing claims)
* '''Safety:''' Inert and insoluble; safe in water. Pink colour can fade in strong sunlight. Facial rollers are fine if cleaned; many cheap 'rose quartz' items are dyed glass.

=== Clear Quartz (Rock Crystal) ===
* '''Mineral:''' Quartz, SiO2 (trigonal); colourless; piezoelectric - used as oscillators in watches and radios; Mohs 7.
* '''Tradition:''' Greek krystallos ('ice') - Pliny believed it was permanently frozen ice; scrying spheres; modern New-Age: crown chakra, 'master healer', Sun/Moon; used as a sacred stone by many Indigenous Australian and American cultures.
* '''History:''' Rock crystal was carved into Fatimid Egyptian ewers (10th-11th c.) and medieval reliquaries, and its piezoelectric property (discovered by the Curies in 1880) makes it the real 'crystal technology' in every quartz clock.<ref>[https://www.mindat.org/min-3337.html Mindat: Quartz (min-3337)]</ref><ref>[https://www.gia.edu/amethyst GIA: Amethyst]</ref>
* '''Evidence:''' tradition-only (no clinical evidence for healing claims); its piezoelectricity is real physics but does not translate to body healing
* '''Safety:''' Inert and safe in water. Clear spheres can focus sunlight and start fires - keep out of windowsills. Cutting/grinding produces respirable crystalline silica dust (silicosis risk) - wet-cut with a respirator.

=== Citrine ===
* '''Mineral:''' Quartz, SiO2; yellow to orange from trace iron; natural citrine is rare - most commercial 'citrine' is heat-treated amethyst or smoky quartz; Mohs 7.
* '''Tradition:''' Modern New-Age: solar plexus chakra, Sun, Gemini/Leo, 'merchant's stone' for prosperity; November birthstone (with topaz).
* '''History:''' Citrine was long confused with topaz in trade, and Art Deco jewellers of the 1920s-30s popularised large heat-treated Brazilian citrines.<ref>[https://www.gia.edu/citrine GIA: Citrine]</ref>
* '''Evidence:''' tradition-only (no clinical evidence for healing claims)
* '''Safety:''' Inert; safe in water. Heat-treated material can fade in prolonged sun.

=== Lapis Lazuli ===
* '''Mineral:''' A rock, not a single mineral: mainly lazurite (Na,Ca)8(AlSiO4)6(S,SO4,Cl)2 (feldspathoid, sodalite group) with white calcite, pyrite flecks, diopside and sodalite; Mohs 5-5.5.
* '''Tradition:''' Sumerian: in 'Inanna's Descent' the goddess carries a lapis-lazuli measuring rod and line and wears lapis beads, stripped from her at the underworld gates; Egyptian: the gods' hair was said to be of lapis (Ra's in the Book of the Heavenly Cow), used in Tutankhamun's funerary mask and scarabs; Abrahamic: the sapphire (sappir) of the Bible is often identified with lapis; modern: throat and third-eye chakras, Jupiter/Venus.
* '''History:''' Nearly all ancient lapis came from the Sar-i Sang mines in Badakhshan, Afghanistan, traded 2,500+ km to the Royal Tombs of Ur (c. 2600 BCE) and to Egypt; ground and purified, it became ultramarine, the most expensive pigment of Renaissance painting.<ref>[https://www.gia.edu/lapis-lazuli GIA: Lapis Lazuli]</ref><ref>[https://etcsl.orinst.ox.ac.uk/section1/tr141.htm ETCSL (Oxford): Inana's descent to the nether world, translation (t.1.4.1)]</ref>
* '''Evidence:''' tradition-only (no clinical evidence for healing claims)
* '''Safety:''' Not for gem waters or elixirs: calcite dissolves in acidic water, pyrite oxidises, and lazurite releases hydrogen sulfide in acid. Often dyed or reconstituted - colour can rub off. Avoid acids and ultrasonic cleaners.

=== Carnelian ===
* '''Mineral:''' Chalcedony (microcrystalline quartz), SiO2, coloured orange-red by iron oxides (hematite/goethite); often heat-enhanced; Mohs 6.5-7.
* '''Tradition:''' Egyptian: red stones like carnelian were linked with the blood of Isis (tyet amulet) and with life/vitality; heart amulets and inlay in Tutankhamun's jewellery; Islamic: Prophet's signet ring tradition (aqiq); modern: sacral chakra, Mars/Sun, Leo/Virgo.
* '''History:''' Carnelian was the most common gemstone of ancient Egypt, and the Harappan (Indus Valley) civilisation exported distinctive etched carnelian beads to Mesopotamia by about 2500 BCE.<ref>[https://the-past.com/feature/the-great-carnelian-mystery/ The Past (Ancient Egypt magazine): The great carnelian mystery]</ref>
* '''Evidence:''' tradition-only (no clinical evidence for healing claims)
* '''Safety:''' Inert; safe in water. Much modern 'carnelian' is dyed agate.

=== Turquoise ===
* '''Mineral:''' Hydrated copper aluminium phosphate, CuAl6(PO4)4(OH)8·4H2O (triclinic); porous; Mohs 5-6.
* '''Tradition:''' Egyptian: Hathor was 'Lady of Turquoise' (nebet mefkat), worshipped at the turquoise mines of Serabit el-Khadim in Sinai; Persian: Nishapur turquoise as a protective stone; Aztec: xihuitl, sacred to the fire god Xiuhtecuhtli, used in mosaic masks; Diné (Navajo) and Puebloan sacred stone of sky and water; modern: throat chakra, Jupiter/Venus, Sagittarius; December birthstone.
* '''History:''' Egyptians mined Sinai turquoise from the First Dynasty onward, and the Hathor temple at Serabit el-Khadim holds the Proto-Sinaitic inscriptions, among the earliest alphabetic writing.<ref>[https://www.gia.edu/turquoise GIA: Turquoise]</ref><ref>[https://www.metmuseum.org/en/perspectives/egyptian-turquoise-third-intermediate-period The Met: Turquoise, Trade, and Statuary in Ancient Egypt (Third Intermediate Period)]</ref>
* '''Evidence:''' tradition-only (no clinical evidence for healing claims)
* '''Safety:''' Contains copper - do not make gem waters or elixirs. Porous: absorbs oils, perfume and skin acids and changes colour; most market turquoise is stabilised with resin, dyed, or is dyed howlite/magnesite.

=== Obsidian ===
* '''Mineral:''' Natural volcanic glass, amorphous (not a mineral), roughly 70-75% SiO2 rhyolitic composition; conchoidal fracture; Mohs 5-5.5.
* '''Tradition:''' Aztec: Tezcatlipoca ('Smoking Mirror') and obsidian scrying mirrors; Elizabethan magus John Dee's 'magic mirror' (now in the British Museum) is Aztec obsidian from Pachuca, Mexico; modern: root chakra, Saturn/Pluto, Scorpio, 'protection' stone.
* '''History:''' Obsidian was the premier blade material of the Stone Age, traded across the Neolithic Near East from Anatolian sources, and Mesoamerican macuahuitl swords were edged with it; a 2021 study confirmed John Dee's mirror is Mexican obsidian.<ref>[https://www.smithsonianmag.com/smart-news/magic-mirror-used-by-queen-elizabeth-is-court-astrologer-has-aztec-origins-180978830/ Smithsonian Magazine: Magic mirror used by Queen Elizabeth I's court astrologer has Aztec origins]</ref>
* '''Evidence:''' tradition-only (no clinical evidence for healing claims); obsidian blade edges are genuinely sharper than steel scalpels and have been trialled in surgery
* '''Safety:''' Fractured edges are razor-sharp; knapping throws glass shards - eye protection and gloves; glass dust is irritating. Inert in water.

=== Moonstone ===
* '''Mineral:''' Feldspar - microscopic intergrowth of orthoclase (KAlSi3O8) and albite (NaAlSi3O8) layers that scatter light (adularescence); Mohs 6-6.5, perfect cleavage.
* '''Tradition:''' Moon; Roman belief (Pliny) that it formed from solidified moonlight and changed with lunar phases; in India regarded as sacred and auspicious; modern: crown/sacral chakra, Cancer; June birthstone (with pearl and alexandrite).
* '''History:''' Romans used moonstone in jewellery believing it was moonlight made solid, and Art Nouveau jewellers such as Rene Lalique made it fashionable around 1900; Sri Lanka has been the classic source.<ref>[https://www.gia.edu/moonstone GIA: Moonstone]</ref>
* '''Evidence:''' tradition-only (no clinical evidence for healing claims)
* '''Safety:''' Inert and safe in water, but cleaves easily - avoid knocks, heat and ultrasonic cleaners.

=== Malachite ===
* '''Mineral:''' Copper carbonate hydroxide, Cu2CO3(OH)2 (monoclinic carbonate); banded green; Mohs 3.5-4; soluble in acids.
* '''Tradition:''' Egyptian: ground malachite was green eye paint (wadj) with protective meaning, and Hathor was also called 'Lady of Malachite' at Sinai; Venus/copper association in alchemy; modern: heart chakra, Scorpio/Capricorn, 'protection' stone.
* '''History:''' Malachite was among the first copper ores smelted (Sinai, Timna, 4th millennium BCE), and Russian Ural malachite veneered the Malachite Room of the Winter Palace, St Petersburg.<ref>[https://www.gemsociety.org/article/malachite-jewelry-and-gemstone-information/ International Gem Society: Malachite value, price and jewelry information (toxicity/lapidary notes)]</ref><ref>[https://www.mindat.org/min-2550.html Mindat: Malachite (min-2550)]</ref>
* '''Evidence:''' tradition-only (no clinical evidence for healing claims)
* '''Safety:''' TOXIC: never make malachite gem waters or elixirs, and never ingest - it releases soluble copper in acidic liquids (vomiting, liver/kidney damage). Cutting or polishing dust is a copper inhalation hazard - wet-work and respirator. Finished, sealed jewellery is fine to wear; keep away from water, acids and perfume.

=== Garnet ===
* '''Mineral:''' Group of nesosilicates X3Y2(SiO4)3 - e.g. pyrope Mg3Al2(SiO4)3, almandine Fe3Al2(SiO4)3, spessartine, grossular, andradite (demantoid), uvarovite; cubic; Mohs 6.5-7.5.
* '''Tradition:''' Name from Latin granatum (pomegranate seed); legend that Noah lit the Ark with a garnet; carbuncle of the Bible; modern: root chakra, Mars, Capricorn/Aquarius; January birthstone.
* '''History:''' Garnet cloisonne set in gold is the signature of Anglo-Saxon royal treasure at Sutton Hoo and in the Staffordshire Hoard, much of it from garnets traded from India and Sri Lanka.<ref>[https://www.gia.edu/garnet GIA: Garnet]</ref>
* '''Evidence:''' tradition-only (no clinical evidence for healing claims)
* '''Safety:''' Insoluble and inert; safe in water. Industrial garnet abrasive dust should not be inhaled.

=== Jade (Nephrite and Jadeite) ===
* '''Mineral:''' Two different minerals: nephrite, an amphibole (tremolite-actinolite, Ca2(Mg,Fe)5Si8O22(OH)2), Mohs 6-6.5, extremely tough; and jadeite, a pyroxene (NaAlSi2O6), Mohs 6.5-7.
* '''Tradition:''' Chinese yu: the 'stone of heaven', embodying Confucian virtues (benevolence, integrity, wisdom), bi discs (heaven) and cong tubes (earth) in Neolithic burials, Han jade burial suits; Maori pounamu (nephrite) taonga; Olmec and Maya jadeite as breath/soul; modern: heart chakra, Venus, Taurus/Libra.
* '''History:''' Liangzhu culture carved nephrite cong and bi around 3300-2300 BCE without metal tools, and the British Museum holds a cong of c. 2500 BCE; jadeite from Burma only reached China in the 18th century.<ref>[https://www.gia.edu/jade GIA: Jade]</ref><ref>[https://www.britishmuseum.org/collection/object/A_1945-1017-157 British Museum collection: Liangzhu nephrite cong, c. 2500 BC (1945,1017.157)]</ref>
* '''Evidence:''' tradition-only (no clinical evidence for healing claims)
* '''Safety:''' Inert and safe in water. Many 'jade' pieces are dyed or polymer-impregnated (B/C-grade) or are serpentine, aventurine or glass. Cutting raw nephrite/tremolite: wet-cut, as fibrous amphibole dust is a lung hazard.

=== Emerald ===
* '''Mineral:''' Beryl, Be3Al2Si6O18 (hexagonal cyclosilicate) coloured green by chromium and/or vanadium; Mohs 7.5-8 but brittle with inclusions ('jardin').
* '''Tradition:''' Venus; Egyptian 'Cleopatra's mines' (Mons Smaragdus, Wadi Sikait) in the Eastern Desert; Inca and Muisca sacred stone (Colombian Muzo/Chivor); Islamic Mughal carved emeralds with Quranic verses; the 'Emerald Tablet' of Hermes Trismegistus; modern: heart chakra, Taurus/Cancer; May birthstone.
* '''History:''' Emeralds were mined in Egypt's Eastern Desert from the Ptolemaic and Roman period, but after the Spanish conquest Colombian emeralds flooded Mughal India and Ottoman Turkey.<ref>[https://www.gia.edu/emerald GIA: Emerald]</ref>
* '''Evidence:''' tradition-only (no clinical evidence for healing claims)
* '''Safety:''' Most emeralds are oiled or resin-filled - avoid hot water, solvents, ultrasonic and steam cleaning. Beryl contains beryllium: cutting dust is hazardous (berylliosis) - lapidary only with wet methods and extraction; handling finished stones is safe.

=== Bloodstone (Heliotrope) ===
* '''Mineral:''' Dark-green chalcedony or jasper (cryptocrystalline SiO2) coloured by chlorite/hornblende inclusions, with red spots of iron oxide (hematite); Mohs 6.5-7.
* '''Tradition:''' Greek heliotropion ('sun-turner'): Pliny wrote that in water it turns sunlight blood-red; Christian legend that the red spots are drops of Christ's blood at the Crucifixion (carved into martyr cameos); Babylonian seals; modern: root/heart chakra, Mars, Aries/Pisces; March birthstone (with aquamarine).
* '''History:''' Bloodstone, chiefly from the Deccan Traps of India, was carved as seals and signet rings from antiquity and as devotional cameos of the Passion in medieval and Renaissance Europe.<ref>[https://www.gemdat.org/gem-7616.html Gemdat: Bloodstone (Heliotrope)]</ref>
* '''Evidence:''' tradition-only (no clinical evidence for healing claims); its old use to 'stop bleeding' has no basis
* '''Safety:''' Inert and safe in water.

== Diagrams ==

* '''The Seven Planets: metals, gems and herbs''': How the classical correspondence system links each planet to a metal, a Navaratna gem, a weekday, a god in four cultures and Culpeper's herbs. ''(tradition (correspondence system; not a medical claim))''
* '''The liver's enzyme crossroads (CYP450)''': Why herbs interact with drugs: inducers (St John's wort -> CYP3A4/P-gp up, drugs fail) vs inhibitors (grapefruit, goldenseal, piperine, high-dose curcumin -> drug levels rise). ''(established pharmacology)''
* '''TCM Five Phases (Wu Xing)''': Wood-Liver, Fire-Heart, Earth-Spleen, Metal-Lung, Water-Kidney; herbs are classed by nature (cold-hot) and five flavours. ''(traditional framework)''
* '''Ayurveda: the three doshas''': Vata, Pitta, Kapha and the six tastes (rasa); how warming herbs (ginger) and cooling herbs (amla, coriander) are chosen. ''(traditional framework)''
* '''Unani / Galenic four humours''': Unani Tibb (Ibn Sina's Canon) classes herbs as hot/cold and dry/moist by degree; black seed, rose, fennel, senna. ''(traditional framework)''
* '''Enzymes in the kitchen''': Proteolytic food enzymes: bromelain (pineapple), papain (papaya), actinidin (kiwi), zingibain (ginger); honey's glucose oxidase makes hydrogen peroxide (why honey dressings work). ''(established biochemistry)''
* '''The old wives' medicine cabinet''': Folk remedies with real support: honey for cough (not under 1 year), ginger for nausea, peppermint oil for IBS, clove (eugenol) for toothache, salt-water gargle, aloe for minor burns. ''(mixed: several established, see each herb card)''
* '''How it all goes together''': Plants = chemistry you can test; gems and planets = the symbolic grammar old healers used to remember it; gods = the stories that carried the knowledge. ''(framework; chemistry claims are on the herb cards)''
* '''A sleep tea, taken apart''': Chamomile (apigenin, GABA-A), lemon balm (rosmarinic acid, GABA-transaminase inhibition), valerian (valerenic acid); additive with sedatives and alcohol. ''(traditional-with-some-evidence)''
* '''The doctrine of signatures (and why it misleads)''': Paracelsus/Boehme: a plant's shape shows its use. Historically important, medically unreliable; a teaching card on testing claims. ''(historical idea; not evidence)''
* '''Hathor's herb index''': Ask Hathor: every card links to the wiki article with doses, sources and interaction warnings. ''(n/a)''
